title: Identifying Supply and Demand Elasticities of Agricultural Commodities: Implications for the US Ethanol Mandate
research_question: How do supply and demand for the world's major staple food commodities (corn, rice, soybeans, and wheat) respond to price changes, and how much has the U.S. Renewable Fuel Standard mandate—diverting a substantial share of grain production into ethanol—raised global food commodity prices, expanded cropland, and reduced food consumers' surplus?
data_description: The study uses annual global data from 1961-2010 on the four staple commodities: maize, rice, soybeans, and wheat. Production, area harvested, yields, and stock variation come from the FAO of the United Nations (baseline, through 2007 for inventories) and from the USDA Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS, sensitivity check). Quantities are converted to caloric equivalents using Williamson and Williamson (1942) conversion factors and aggregated globally. Price data are monthly futures prices from the Chicago Board of Trade (December delivery for corn/wheat, November for soybeans/rice), deflated by the U.S. CPI; longer historical farm prices come from USDA NASS. Weather data (monthly temperature and precipitation on a 0.5-degree grid, 1901-2008) are from the University of Delaware Center for Climatic Research. Country-level yields are modeled for each country averaging at least 0.5% of world production for a given crop; growing-season weather is computed using crop calendars and area weights from Monfreda et al. (2008) and Sacks et al. (2010). The unit of observation is the crop-year at the global aggregate level.
institutional_context: Between 2005 and 2008, prices of the four staple grains roughly quadrupled, sparking debate about the drivers of food inflation, hunger in developing countries, and indirect land-use change. A central policy development was the rapid expansion of U.S. corn-based ethanol, supported by ethanol tax credits, restrictions on ethanol imports, and a sequence of federal renewable fuel mandates: the 2005 Energy Policy Act, the 2007 Energy Independence and Security Act, and especially the 2009 Renewable Fuel Standard, which required blending roughly 11 billion gallons of ethanol into gasoline. Meeting this mandate consumed about one-third of U.S. corn production—approximately 5% of global caloric production from corn, wheat, rice, and soybeans combined. Because the U.S. accounts for around 23% of world caloric production of these staples (and roughly 40% of world maize), this policy-driven demand shift has global consequences for commodity prices, cropland expansion (with implications for deforestation and CO2 emissions), and welfare distribution between net food-importing and exporting nations.
